title: September's unusual heat takes a toll on Bengalureans - Deccan Herald
full_text:
“There is a noticeable increase in patients reporting heat-related symptoms during unusually warm or humid periods in September compared with a typical September,” said Dr Brunda MS, Senior Consultant, Internal Medicine. Persistent heat, humidity and inadequate fluid intake can contribute to such problems, she added.
Kiran Chandrashekar, Consultant, General Medicine, said September had seen fewer significant rainy days than usual, contributing to viral infections and other illnesses. “Recovery days have also become longer as fatigue is prolonged due to heat,” he said.
Doctors said weather variations can affect the persistence of respiratory droplets and aerosols and the survival of some viruses. However, respiratory viruses continue to spread primarily through close contact and respiratory droplets or aerosols, said Dr Vivek Anand Padegal, Director of Pulmonology at a private hospital.
Dr Arvinda SN, Lead Consultant, said heat-related fatigue, muscle cramps and dizziness on standing had become common. Heat can affect blood flow and blood pressure, causing dizziness, he said.
He advised people to watch whether symptoms improve with rest and cooling. Persistent or worsening symptoms should not be dismissed as routine fatigue.
Unlike April and May, when hot weather is expected, people may underestimate the risk in September, doctors said. Symptoms during the month are more likely to occur on particularly hot or humid days rather than persist throughout the period.
